question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The manager and him (a)/ have been asked to (b)/ present the annual report (c)/ before the board of directors. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error lies in the case of the pronoun. A pronoun that forms part of the subject must be in the nominative (subjective) case — I, we, you, he, she, they. The objective forms — me, us, him, her, them — are used only for objects.

 

• Here the compound subject is "The manager and …" and it takes the verb "have been asked". So the pronoun must be "he", not "him".

◦ Corrected sentence: The manager and he have been asked to present the annual report before the board of directors.

 

• A quick test: drop the first noun and read the pronoun alone. Him have been asked is clearly wrong, while He has been asked is right.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "have been asked to" is a present perfect passive whose plural verb agrees with a compound subject joined by "and".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "present the annual report" is a proper verb–object phrase following the infinitive "to".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "before the board of directors" is a properly formed prepositional phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• Compound subjects take nominative pronouns: Rahul and I went to the fair (not "Rahul and me"). Compound objects take objective pronouns: The teacher praised Rahul and me (not "Rahul and I").

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The organisation decided to raise their membership fee to meet its rising expenses.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. its membership fee.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A collective or institutional noun such as organisation, company, bank, committee or government is treated as a singular unit when it acts as one body. The pronoun referring back to it must therefore be the singular possessive "its", not the plural "their".

 

• The sentence already uses "its rising expenses" later on, which confirms that "organisation" is being treated as singular; the earlier pronoun must be consistent with it.

◦ Corrected sentence: The organisation decided to raise its membership fee to meet its rising expenses.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "it's membership fee" — "it's" is only the contraction of "it is / it has" and can never be possessive. The possessive form is "its" (no apostrophe).

 

• Option 2: No substitution required — cannot be right because the plural "their" does not agree with the singular "organisation" and clashes with "its" used later in the same sentence.

 

• Option 4: "their membership fees" — still uses the plural "their", so the error is not removed.

 

NOTE

 

• its = belonging to it (The dog wagged its tail); it's = it is / it has (It's raining). SSC often tests this pair together with their / there / they're.

 

• A collective noun takes a plural pronoun only when its members are thought of as separate individuals (The committee were divided in their opinions); when the group acts as one unit, use "it / its".

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The head of the department was impressed by Anita and I.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. by Anita and me.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A pronoun that follows a preposition (by, with, for, to, between, from, about, etc.) is the object of that preposition and must be in the objective case — me, us, him, her, them. "I" is the nominative (subject) form and cannot be the object of "by".

 

• Joining the pronoun to another noun with "and" does not change its case. The correct form is therefore "by Anita and me".

◦ Corrected sentence: The head of the department was impressed by Anita and me.

◦ Test: remove "Anita and" — impressed by I is clearly wrong, whereas impressed by me is right.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "with Anita and I" — the preposition changes but "I" still stands in the wrong (nominative) case.

 

• Option 2: No substitution required — incorrect, because "I" cannot follow a preposition.

 

• Option 3: "by I and Anita" — "I" is still governed by "by" and is wrongly nominative; changing the word order does not change the case.

 

NOTE

 

• Classic SSC traps: between you and me (never "between you and I"), everyone except him and me, let him and me handle it. Prepositions such as between, except, but, like, with, for always take the objective case.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

We should always be careful about how we treat our colleagues because it shapes your reputation at the workplace.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. shapes our reputation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A pronoun must agree in person (first, second or third) with the subject it refers to. The sentence begins with "We" (first person plural) and speaks of "our colleagues", so the later possessive must also be first person plural — "our".

 

• A sudden shift to "your" (second person) is called a person shift and is treated as an error in SSC.

◦ Corrected sentence: We should always be careful about how we treat our colleagues because it shapes our reputation at the workplace.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "shape their reputation" — the plural verb "shape" does not agree with the singular "it", and "their" moves to the third person.

 

• Option 3: "shapes his reputation" — "his" is third person masculine singular with no antecedent in the sentence.

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because "your" creates a person shift from "we".

 

NOTE

 

• Keep the person consistent: If you work hard, you will succeed (not "he will succeed"); One must do one's duty (not "his" or "your").

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Those keys are not ours; they must be her's.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. hers.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Possessive pronouns — mine, ours, yours, his, hers, theirs — stand on their own in place of a "possessive adjective + noun" and are never written with an apostrophe. The correct feminine form is "hers".

 

• "her" is a possessive adjective and always needs a noun after it (her keys). It cannot end the sentence as "they must be her"; "hers" completes the sense (= her keys).

◦ Corrected sentence: Those keys are not ours; they must be hers.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "her" — a possessive adjective that requires a noun after it, so the sentence is incomplete.

 

• Option 2: "hers'" — a superfluous apostrophe; possessive pronouns never take one.

 

• Option 4: "she's" — the contraction of "she is / she has", which makes no sense here (they must be she is).

 

NOTE

 

• No apostrophe in ours, yours, hers, theirs, its. Do not confuse whose (possessive) with who's (who is / who has).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Please complete the paperwork first and then send I the copy by email.
option_1: and then send me the copy
option_2: and than send me the copy
option_4: or then sending I the copy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. and then send me the copy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Send" is a transitive verb, and a pronoun used as its object must be in the objective case — "me", not "I".

 

• "Then" is an adverb of time meaning "next / after that" and correctly joins two actions in sequence, whereas "than" is used only in comparisons. So "and then send me the copy" is the correct form.

◦ Corrected sentence: Please complete the paperwork first and then send me the copy by email.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "and than send me the copy" — the pronoun is corrected but "than" is misused; it cannot show sequence.

 

• Option 3: No improvement required — incorrect, because "send I" uses the nominative case for an object.

 

• Option 4: "or then sending I the copy" — the wrong case is retained, and "or" and "sending" also break the structure of the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• First wash your hands, then eat. She is older than her brother. — remember then = time / sequence, than = comparison.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Both of hers daughters have won medals at the national level.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Both of her daughters have.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "hers" is a possessive pronoun that stands alone (The bag is hers). Before a noun we must use the possessive adjective — "her". So "hers daughters" is wrong; "her daughters" is right.

 

• "Both of" refers to two persons or things and is always followed by a plural noun and a plural verb: Both of her daughters have. Hence "daughter" and "has" are wrong.

◦ Corrected sentence: Both of her daughters have won medals at the national level.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Both of hers daughter have" — "hers" is still wrong before a noun, and the singular "daughter" cannot follow "both of".

 

• Option 3: No improvement required — incorrect, because "hers" cannot be placed before a noun.

 

• Option 4: "Both of her daughter has" — the possessive is fixed, but a singular noun and a singular verb are wrongly used after "both of".

 

NOTE

 

• Possessive adjective → possessive pronoun: my–mine, our–ours, your–yours, her–hers, their–theirs (his stays the same).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

It is quite evident (a)/ that her performance in the (b)/ final round was much better (c)/ than your one. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A possessive pronoun (mine, yours, hers, ours, theirs) replaces a "possessive adjective + noun" to avoid repetition. "one" cannot be attached to possessive adjectives such as my, your, her, our or their. So "your one" is wrong and the correct form is "yours" (= your performance).

◦ Corrected sentence: It is quite evident that her performance in the final round was much better than yours.

 

• The comparison is now between like things — "her performance" and "yours" (= your performance).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "It is quite evident" uses the anticipatory "it" correctly.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "that her performance in the" begins the noun clause correctly, and "her" agrees with the antecedent.

 

• Part (c) is correct — the singular verb "was" agrees with "performance", and "much" correctly intensifies the comparative "better".

 

NOTE

 

• my one → mine, their ones → theirs. But "one" is fine after an article, demonstrative or adjective: the red one, this one, a better one.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The gold ring (a)/ that you found near the gate (b)/ might be her, (c)/ so ask her about it. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After the linking verb "be", the sense is "the ring might be her ring". A pronoun that stands for "possessive adjective + noun" is a possessive pronoun — "hers". "Her" is either an objective pronoun or a possessive adjective (which needs a noun), so it is wrong here.

◦ Corrected sentence: The gold ring that you found near the gate might be hers, so ask her about it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The gold ring" is a proper noun phrase acting as the subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "that" is the right relative pronoun for a thing, and "you found near the gate" is a proper relative clause.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "her" here is the object of the verb "ask", so the objective case is right.

 

NOTE

 

• Compare: This is her book (possessive adjective + noun) but This book is hers (possessive pronoun, stands alone).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The municipal corporation (a)/ has decided to renovate (b)/ the old auditorium (c)/ at their own expense. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Corporation" is a body treated as a single unit, and the singular verb "has decided" confirms this. A pronoun referring to a singular non-person noun must be "its", not the plural "their".

◦ Corrected sentence: The municipal corporation has decided to renovate the old auditorium at its own expense.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The municipal corporation" is a proper singular subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — the singular verb "has decided" agrees with "corporation", and "to renovate" is a correct infinitive.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the old auditorium" is a properly formed object.

 

NOTE

 

• The same applies to government, committee, company, bank, team, army acting as one unit: The Government has announced its policy; The team has won its first match.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Learn to (a)/ depend on myself (b)/ if you want (c)/ to succeed in life. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A reflexive pronoun must agree in person and number with the subject of the action. The understood subject of the imperative "Learn to depend on …" is "you", which is confirmed by "if you want". So the reflexive pronoun must be "yourself", not "myself".

◦ Corrected sentence: Learn to depend on yourself if you want to succeed in life.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Learn to" is a proper imperative followed by an infinitive.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "if you want" is a proper conditional clause in the simple present.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "to succeed in life" is a proper infinitive of purpose.

 

NOTE

 

• Reflexive pronouns: myself, ourselves, yourself / yourselves, himself, herself, itself, themselves, oneself — each must match its antecedent: I hurt myself, They blamed themselves.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The Konark Sun Temple (a)/ is one of the (b)/ most magnificent (c)/ monument in India. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The pattern "one of the + superlative + plural noun" is compulsory, because "one of" selects a single item from a group of several. So the singular "monument" must be changed to the plural "monuments".

◦ Corrected sentence: The Konark Sun Temple is one of the most magnificent monuments in India.

 

• The verb stays singular ("is") because it agrees with "one" (and "Temple"), not with the plural noun after "of".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The Konark Sun Temple" is a singular subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — the singular verb "is" agrees with the subject, and "one of the" is the correct beginning of the pattern.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "most magnificent" is the correct superlative form of the adjective.

 

NOTE

 

• One of the boys is absent; Each of the players has a bat; One of my friends lives abroad — after "one of / each of + plural noun", the noun is plural but the verb is singular.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Each of the two contestants (a)/ who reached the final round (b)/ was given a special medal. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct as it stands. "Each of" is followed by a plural noun ("the two contestants") but the verb agrees with the singular subject "Each" — so "was given" is correct.

◦ Sentence as given: Each of the two contestants who reached the final round was given a special medal.

 

• The relative pronoun "who" is correctly used for persons, and the past tense verb in the passive voice is properly formed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Each of the two contestants" is the accepted form of a distributive pronoun followed by a plural noun.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "who reached the final round" is a proper relative clause in the simple past.

 

• Part (c) is correct — the singular passive verb "was given" agrees with "Each".

 

NOTE

 

• Each, every one, either, neither, one take singular verbs even when followed by "of + plural noun": Each of the boys has a book; Either of the roads is safe.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

We tried to contact two of the eyewitnesses but no one of them was available.
option_1: but none of them were available
option_2: but either of them was available
option_3: but neither of them was available
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. but neither of them was available.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a negative statement concerns exactly two persons or things, the correct pronoun is "neither" (= not the one and not the other). "None" and "no one" are used when three or more are involved, and "no one of them" is not a standard construction.

◦ Corrected sentence: We tried to contact two of the eyewitnesses but neither of them was available.

 

• "Neither of" + plural noun / pronoun takes a singular verb in standard usage — "neither of them was".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "but none of them were available" — "none" is used for more than two; the sentence speaks of exactly two eyewitnesses.

 

• Option 2: "but either of them was available" — "either" is positive and reverses the sense; the contrast with "we tried to contact" needs a negative.

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because "no one of them" is not idiomatic for two persons.

 

NOTE

 

• Either / neither / both → two persons or things. Any / none / all → more than two.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the part of the sentence given in brackets.

 

(Each of the players in the squad have been given) a fitness certificate before the tournament.
option_2: Each of the player in the squad have been given
option_3: All of the players in the squad has been given
option_4: Each of the players in the squad has been given
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Each of the players in the squad has been given.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Each of" is followed by a plural noun, but the verb agrees with the singular "Each". So the verb must be "has been given", not "have been given".

◦ Corrected sentence: (Each of the players in the squad has been given) a fitness certificate before the tournament.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: No improvement required — incorrect, because the plural "have" does not agree with the singular "Each".

 

• Option 2: "Each of the player in the squad have been given" — both errors: a singular noun after "each of" and a plural verb.

 

• Option 3: "All of the players in the squad has been given" — "all of" with a plural noun takes a plural verb, so "has" is wrong.

 

NOTE

 

• Singular verb with each, every one, either, neither, one: Each of the students has passed. But All of the students have passed.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

You may choose (a)/ any of the two (b)/ subjects offered (c)/ as an optional paper. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Any" is used for three or more persons or things, whereas "either" is used for two. Since only two subjects are mentioned, the correct phrase is "either of the two".

◦ Corrected sentence: You may choose either of the two subjects offered as an optional paper.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "You may choose" is a proper modal + base verb construction.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "subjects offered" is a proper past participle phrase qualifying the noun.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "as an optional paper" is a proper prepositional phrase with the correct article.

 

NOTE

 

• Either of the two / Neither of the two but any of the three / none of the four — the number of items decides the pronoun.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

None of the volunteer have received any payment for their work.
option_1: None of the volunteers have received
option_2: None of the volunteer has received
option_3: None of the volunteers is received
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. None of the volunteers have received.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "None of" means "not one of a group", so it must be followed by a plural noun or pronoun. The singular "volunteer" after "of the" is therefore wrong; it must be "volunteers".

 

• With a plural noun after "none of the", the plural verb "have received" is the accepted modern usage and matches the plural "their work" later in the sentence.

◦ Corrected sentence: None of the volunteers have received any payment for their work.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "None of the volunteer has received" — the singular noun after "none of the" remains wrong.

 

• Option 3: "None of the volunteers is received" — "is received" is a passive form that makes no sense here.

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because "volunteer" must be plural after "none of the".

 

NOTE

 

• None of + plural noun (None of the boys are present). Use "not one of" or "no one" when the singular sense is to be stressed.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The government has taken several steps to control this rising prices.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. these.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A demonstrative adjective must agree in number with the noun it qualifies: this / that go with singular nouns and these / those with plural nouns. "Prices" is plural, so "these" is required.

◦ Corrected sentence: The government has taken several steps to control these rising prices.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "that" — a singular demonstrative, so the error remains.

 

• Option 2: No substitution required — incorrect, because "this" cannot qualify the plural "prices".

 

• Option 4: "it" — a personal pronoun that cannot be placed before a noun phrase like "rising prices".

 

NOTE

 

• this book / these books, that man / those men. Also this kind of book / these kinds of books.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

No one (a)/ in the office (b)/ can type faster (c)/ than her. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "than" in a comparison, the pronoun is the subject of an understood verb: "No one can type faster than she (can)". In the traditional grammar tested in SSC, the pronoun must therefore be in the nominative case — "she", not "her".

◦ Corrected sentence: No one in the office can type faster than she.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "No one" is a singular indefinite pronoun that agrees with "can".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "in the office" is a proper prepositional phrase.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "can type faster" uses the correct comparative form.

 

NOTE

 

• Complete the sentence mentally: He is taller than I (am). The case depends on the understood verb — She likes him more than me (= more than she likes me) but She likes him more than I (= more than I do).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Sugar and salt are both essential in cooking; (a)/ this makes food sweet (b)/ and that makes it salty. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "This" refers to the latter (the one mentioned last of two) and "that" refers to the former (the one mentioned first). In part (a) the order is "sugar and salt", so the latter is salt and the former is sugar. As written, "this makes food sweet" points to salt — the wrong sense.

 

• The error is removed by interchanging the nouns in (a): Salt and sugar — then this (the latter, sugar) makes food sweet and that (the former, salt) makes it salty.

◦ Corrected sentence: Salt and sugar are both essential in cooking; this makes food sweet and that makes it salty.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — once the order in (a) is set right, "this" rightly points to sugar, the latter.

 

• Part (c) is correct — once the order in (a) is set right, "that" rightly points to salt, the former.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because as written the pronouns point to the wrong nouns.

 

NOTE

 

• This → latter (nearer in the sentence); that → former (farther). Gold and iron are both metals; this (iron) is cheaper than that (gold).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The climate of Shimla (a)/ is much cooler (b)/ than Delhi. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A comparison must be made between like things. Here the "climate of Shimla" is wrongly compared with "Delhi" (a city). To avoid repeating the noun "climate", the singular demonstrative pronoun "that" is used: "than that of Delhi".

◦ Corrected sentence: The climate of Shimla is much cooler than that of Delhi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The climate of Shimla" is a proper singular subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — the singular verb "is" agrees with "climate", and "much cooler" is a proper comparative.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because the comparison in part (c) is illogical.

 

NOTE

 

• Use "that of" for a singular noun and "those of" for a plural noun: The population of India is larger than that of Japan; The roads of Delhi are wider than those of Jaipur.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The salaries offered (a)/ by private banks are (b)/ higher than (c)/ that of public sector banks. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence compares the salaries of private banks with the salaries of public sector banks. To avoid repeating the plural noun, a demonstrative pronoun is used, and it must agree in number: for the plural "salaries" it is "those", not "that".

◦ Corrected sentence: The salaries offered by private banks are higher than those of public sector banks.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The salaries offered" is a plural subject with a proper participle phrase.

 

• Part (b) is correct — the plural verb "are" agrees with "salaries".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "higher than" is a proper comparative structure.

 

NOTE

 

• The rivers of India are longer than those of Bangladesh (plural) but The climate of Shimla is cooler than that of Delhi (singular).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The doctor, (a)/ which treated my father (b)/ last winter, (c)/ has retired from service. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Relative pronouns are chosen by the antecedent: "who" for persons and "which" for animals and things. "Doctor" is a person, so "which" is wrong. Since the pronoun is the subject of "treated", the nominative "who" is required.

◦ Corrected sentence: The doctor, who treated my father last winter, has retired from service.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The doctor," is a proper noun subject followed by a non-defining clause set off by commas.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "last winter," is a proper adverbial of time that closes the non-defining clause.

 

• Part (d) is correct — the present perfect "has retired" agrees with the singular subject.

 

NOTE

 

• who / whom / whose → persons; which / whose → animals and things; that → both, but only in restrictive clauses (never after a comma).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Whom do you (a)/ believe will win (b)/ the gold medal (c)/ in the marathon? (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In this question, "do you believe" is merely a parenthetical insertion. The interrogative pronoun is the subject of "will win", so it must be in the nominative case — "Who", not "Whom".

◦ Corrected sentence: Who do you believe will win the gold medal in the marathon?

 

• A test: answer the question — You believe he will win. Since "he" (nominative) fits, use "who".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "believe will win" correctly links the parenthetical verb with the future verb.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the gold medal" is a proper object phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "in the marathon?" is a proper prepositional phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• Substitution test: if he / she / they can replace the pronoun, use who; if him / her / them fits, use whom — Whom did you invite? (you invited him).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The saint, to who the villagers turned for guidance, lived in a small hut.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. to whom.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A relative pronoun that is the object of a preposition must be in the objective case — "whom". The clause means "the villagers turned to him for guidance", so the pronoun after "to" must be "whom".

◦ Corrected sentence: The saint, to whom the villagers turned for guidance, lived in a small hut.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "to whose" — "whose" is possessive and needs a noun after it, which is missing here.

 

• Option 2: "to which" — "which" is used for animals and things, not for a person such as a saint.

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because "who" is nominative and cannot follow the preposition "to".

 

NOTE

 

• Preposition + whom: the man with whom I worked, the girl of whom he spoke, the teacher from whom I learnt.
